rag.name: Mathlib.Notation3.notation3
rag.content:
/--
`notation3` declares notation using Lean-3-style syntax.

Examples:
```
notation3 "∀ᶠ " (...) " in " f ", " r:(scoped p => Filter.eventually p f) => r
notation3 "MyList[" (x", "* => foldr (a b => MyList.cons a b) MyList.nil) "]" => x
```
By default notation is unable to mention any variables defined using `variable`, but
`local notation3` is able to use such local variables.

Use `notation3 (prettyPrint := false)` to keep the command from generating a pretty printer
for the notation.

This command can be used in mathlib4 but it has an uncertain future and was created primarily
for backward compatibility.
-/
elab (name := notation3) doc:(docComment)? attrs?:(Parser.Term.attributes)? attrKind:Term.attrKind
    "notation3" prec?:(precedence)? name?:(namedName)? prio?:(namedPrio)?
    pp?:(ppSpace prettyPrintOpt)? items:(ppSpace notation3Item)+ " => " val:term : command => do
  -- We use raw `Name`s for variables. This maps variable names back to the
  -- identifiers that appear in `items`
  let mut boundIdents : Std.HashMap Name Ident := {}
  -- Replacements to use for the `macro`
  let mut boundValues : Std.HashMap Name Syntax := {}
  -- The names of the bound names in order, used when constructing patterns for delaboration.
  let mut boundNames : Array Name := #[]
  -- The normal/foldl/foldr type of each variable (for delaborator)
  let mut boundType : Std.HashMap Name BoundValueType := {}
  -- Function to update `syntaxArgs` and `pattArgs` using `macroArg` syntax
  let pushMacro (syntaxArgs : Array (TSyntax `stx)) (pattArgs : Array Syntax)
      (mac : TSyntax ``macroArg) := do
    let (syntaxArg, pattArg) ← expandMacroArg mac
    return (syntaxArgs.push syntaxArg, pattArgs.push pattArg)
  -- Arguments for the `syntax` command
  let mut syntaxArgs := #[]
  -- Arguments for the LHS pattern in the `macro`. Also used to construct the syntax
  -- when delaborating
  let mut pattArgs := #[]
  -- The matchers to assemble into a delaborator
  let mut matchers := #[]
  -- Whether we've seen a `(...)` item
  let mut hasBindersItem := false
  -- Whether we've seen a `scoped` item
  let mut hasScoped := false
  for item in items do
    match item with
    | `(notation3Item| $lit:str) =>
      -- Can't use `pushMacro` since it inserts an extra variable into the pattern for `str`, which
      -- breaks our delaborator
      syntaxArgs := syntaxArgs.push (← `(stx| $lit:str))
      pattArgs := pattArgs.push <| mkAtomFrom lit lit.1.isStrLit?.get!
    | `(notation3Item| $_:bindersItem) =>
      if hasBindersItem then
        throwErrorAt item "Cannot have more than one `(...)` item."
      hasBindersItem := true
      -- HACK: Lean 3 traditionally puts a space after the main binder atom, resulting in
      -- notation3 "∑ "(...)", "r:(scoped f => sum f) => r
      -- but extBinders already has a space before it so we strip the trailing space of "∑ "
      if let `(stx| $lit:str) := syntaxArgs.back! then
        syntaxArgs := syntaxArgs.pop.push (← `(stx| $(quote lit.getString.trimRight):str))
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs (← `(macroArg| binders:extBinders))
    | `(notation3Item| ($id:ident $sep:str* $(prec?)? => $kind ($x $y => $scopedTerm) $init)) =>
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs <| ←
        `(macroArg| $id:ident:sepBy(term $(prec?)?, $sep:str))
      -- N.B. `Syntax.getId` returns `.anonymous` for non-idents
      let scopedTerm' ← scopedTerm.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
      let init' ← init.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
      boundIdents := boundIdents.insert id.getId id
      match kind with
        | `(foldKind| foldl) =>
          boundValues := boundValues.insert id.getId <| ←
            `(expand_foldl% ($x $y => $scopedTerm') $init' [$$(.ofElems $id),*])
          boundNames := boundNames.push id.getId
          boundType := boundType.insert id.getId .foldl
          matchers := matchers.push <|
            mkFoldlMatcher id.getId x.getId y.getId scopedTerm init boundNames
        | `(foldKind| foldr) =>
          boundValues := boundValues.insert id.getId <| ←
            `(expand_foldr% ($x $y => $scopedTerm') $init' [$$(.ofElems $id),*])
          boundNames := boundNames.push id.getId
          boundType := boundType.insert id.getId .foldr
          matchers := matchers.push <|
            mkFoldrMatcher id.getId x.getId y.getId scopedTerm init boundNames
        | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
    | `(notation3Item| $lit:ident $(prec?)? : (scoped $scopedId:ident => $scopedTerm)) =>
      hasScoped := true
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs <|←
        `(macroArg| $lit:ident:term $(prec?)?)
      matchers := matchers.push <|
        mkScopedMatcher lit.getId scopedId.getId scopedTerm boundNames
      let scopedTerm' ← scopedTerm.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
      boundIdents := boundIdents.insert lit.getId lit
      boundValues := boundValues.insert lit.getId <| ←
        `(expand_binders% ($scopedId => $scopedTerm') $$binders:extBinders,
          $(⟨lit.1.mkAntiquotNode `term⟩):term)
      boundNames := boundNames.push lit.getId
    | `(notation3Item| $lit:ident $(prec?)?) =>
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs <|←
        `(macroArg| $lit:ident:term $(prec?)?)
      boundIdents := boundIdents.insert lit.getId lit
      boundValues := boundValues.insert lit.getId <| lit.1.mkAntiquotNode `term
      boundNames := boundNames.push lit.getId
    | _stx => throwUnsupportedSyntax
  if hasScoped && !hasBindersItem then
    throwError "If there is a `scoped` item then there must be a `(...)` item for binders."

  -- 1. The `syntax` command
  let name ← mkNameFromSyntax name? syntaxArgs attrKind
  elabCommand <| ← `(command|
    $[$doc]? $(attrs?)? $attrKind
    syntax $(prec?)? (name := $(Lean.mkIdent name)) $(prio?)? $[$syntaxArgs]* : term)

  -- 2. The `macro_rules`
  let currNamespace : Name ← getCurrNamespace
  -- The `syntax` command puts definitions into the current namespace; we need this
  -- to make the syntax `pat`.
  let fullName := currNamespace ++ name
  trace[notation3] "syntax declaration has name {fullName}"
  let pat : Term := ⟨mkNode fullName pattArgs⟩
  let val' ← val.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
  let mut macroDecl ← `(macro_rules | `($pat) => `($val'))
  if isLocalAttrKind attrKind then
    -- For local notation, take section variables into account
    macroDecl ← `(section set_option quotPrecheck.allowSectionVars true $macroDecl end)
  elabCommand macroDecl

  -- 3. Create a delaborator
  if getPrettyPrintOpt pp? then
    matchers := matchers.push <| Mathlib.Notation3.mkExprMatcher val boundNames
    -- The matchers need to run in reverse order, so may as well reverse them here.
    let matchersM? := (matchers.reverse.mapM id).run
    -- We let local notations have access to `variable` declarations
    let matchers? ← if isLocalAttrKind attrKind then
      runTermElabM fun _ => matchersM?
    else
      liftTermElabM matchersM?
    if let some ms := matchers? then
      trace[notation3] "Matcher creation succeeded; assembling delaborator"
      let matcher ← ms.foldrM (fun m t => `($(m.2) >=> $t)) (← `(pure))
      trace[notation3] "matcher:{indentD matcher}"
      let mut result ← `(withHeadRefIfTagAppFns `($pat))
      for (name, id) in boundIdents.toArray do
        match boundType.getD name .normal with
        | .normal => result ← `(MatchState.delabVar s $(quote name) (some e) >>= fun $id => $result)
        | .foldl => result ←
          `(let $id := (MatchState.getFoldArray s $(quote name)).reverse; $result)
        | .foldr => result ←
          `(let $id := MatchState.getFoldArray s $(quote name); $result)
      if hasBindersItem then
        result ← `(`(extBinders| $$(MatchState.getBinders s)*) >>= fun binders => $result)
      let delabKeys : List DelabKey := ms.foldr (·.1 ++ ·) []
      for key in delabKeys do
        trace[notation3] "Creating delaborator for key {repr key}"
        let delabName := name ++ Name.mkSimple s!"delab_{key.key}"
        let bodyCore ← `(getExpr >>= fun e => $matcher MatchState.empty >>= fun s => $result)
        let body ←
          match key with
          | .app _ arity => ``(withOverApp $(quote arity) $bodyCore)
          | _            => pure bodyCore
        elabCommand <| ← `(
          /-- Pretty printer defined by `notation3` command. -/
          def $(Lean.mkIdent delabName) : Delab :=
            whenPPOption getPPNotation <| whenNotPPOption getPPExplicit <| $body
          -- Avoid scope issues by adding attribute afterwards.
          attribute [$attrKind delab $(mkIdent key.key)] $(Lean.mkIdent delabName))
        trace[notation3] "Defined delaborator {currNamespace ++ delabName}"
    else
      logWarning s!"\
        Was not able to generate a pretty printer for this notation. \
        If you do not expect it to be pretty printable, then you can use \
        `notation3 (prettyPrint := false)`. \
        If the notation expansion refers to section variables, be sure to do `local notation3`. \
        Otherwise, you might be able to adjust the notation expansion to make it matchable; \
        pretty printing relies on deriving an expression matcher from the expansion. \
        (Use `set_option trace.notation3 true` to get some debug information.)"

variable {β α : Type*} [Collection β α]
informal_statement: For any propositions \( a \) and \( b \), the conjunction \( a \land b \) is logically equivalent to \( b \land a \).
informal_proof:
First, we consider arbitrary propositions \( a \) and \( b \). 
To establish the equivalence \( a \land b \leftrightarrow b \land a \), we will demonstrate both directions:
1. Assume \( a \land b \) holds true.
2. By the definition of conjunction, both \( a \) and \( b \) must be true.
3. Since \( b \) and \( a \) are both true, \( b \land a \) is necessarily true.
4. Conversely, assume \( b \land a \) holds true.
5. Again, by the definition of conjunction, both \( b \) and \( a \) must be true.
6. Therefore, \( a \) and \( b \) are true, making \( a \land b \) true as well.
7. Hence, \( a \land b \) and \( b \land a \) imply each other, proving their logical equivalence.

namespace Collection

variable {β α : Type*} [Collection β α]
informal_statement: For any element `a` of type `α` and any set `s` of type `Set α`, the operation `cons a s` is equal to `insert a s`.
informal_proof: The operation `cons a s` adds the element `a` to the set `s`, resulting in a new set that contains all the elements of `s` along with `a`. Similarly, the operation `insert a s` also adds the element `a` to the set `s` to form a new set containing all elements of `s` plus `a`. Since both operations are defined in a identical way—they both take an existing set and include a specific element within it—they must produce the same result. Therefore, `cons a s` is equal to `insert a s` by definition.

informal_statement: For any element $x$ and any finite set $s$, $x$ is a member of the collection obtained from converting $s$ if and only if $x$ is a member of the original set $s$.
informal_proof: Since `toCollection` is designed to maintain membership without altering the elements, the membership of $x$ in $s$ is preserved when converting to a collection. Therefore, $x$ being in $s$ directly implies it is in the `toCollection`, and vice versa, establishing the equivalence.

namespace Collection

variable {β α : Type*} [Collection β α]
informal_statement: For any element `x` and a list `l`, `x` is in the collection of `l` if and only if `x` is in `l`.
informal_proof:
We will prove that for any element `x` and a list `l`, `x` is in the collection of `l` if and only if `x` is in `l`. This can be shown using induction on the list `l`.

**Base Case:**

When `l` is an empty list, its collection is also empty. Therefore, `x` cannot be in either the collection or the list, making the statement trivially true.

**Inductive Step:**

Assume that the statement holds for a list `l`. We need to show it holds for `l' = l + [x]` (i.e., `l` with an element `x` appended).

- **Case 1:** If `x` was already in `l`, then `x` is in `l'`. Since the collection of `l'` includes all elements of the collection of `l` plus `x` if it wasn't already there, and `x` was in `l`, it is also in the collection of `l'`.

- **Case 2:** If `x` was not in `l`, then `x` is added to the collection of `l'`. Thus, `x` is in the collection of `l'`.

In both cases, `x` is in the collection of `l'` if and only if `x` is in `l'`, maintaining the truth of the statement.

By induction, the statement holds for all lists `l`.

informal_statement: The `toCollection` function converts a list of type `β` into a set of type `α`. It operates by recursively processing each element of the list, ensuring that each element is included in the resulting set exactly once.
informal_proof:
We will prove by mathematical induction on the structure of the list that the function `toCollection` correctly converts a list of type `β` into a set of type `α`.

**Base Case:**
When the list is empty, the function returns the empty set of type `α`. That is, `toCollection [] = ∅`. This holds by definition.

**Inductive Step:**
Assume that for a list `xs` of type `List β`, the function `toCollection xs` correctly returns the corresponding set of type `α`. Now, consider a non-empty list `x :: xs`. By the definition of `toCollection`, we have:
```
toCollection (x :: xs) = x ∈ α ?_ : toCollection xs
```
By the inductive hypothesis, `toCollection xs` correctly represents the set of elements in `xs`. Adding `x` to `toCollection xs` results in a set that includes `x` along with all elements of `xs`, which correctly represents the set corresponding to the list `x :: xs`.

Thus, by induction, the function `toCollection` correctly converts any list of type `β` into a set of type `α`.

informal_statement: The function `addList` takes an initial value `a` and a list `β`, then it appends all elements of the list to `a`.
informal_proof:
To understand the behavior of the function `addList`, let's break it down step by step.

1. **Base Case**: If the input list is empty (`[]`), the function directly returns the initial value `a`. This is straightforward as there are no elements to append.

2. **Recursive Case**: If the list is not empty, it is represented as `x :: xs`, where `x` is the first element of the list, and `xs` is the rest of the list. The function performs two main operations:
   - It appends the first element `x` to `a`, resulting in `cons x (addList a xs)`.
   - It then recursively processes the rest of the list `xs` using the same logic.

3. **Inductive Step**: By applying the recursive definition, each element of the list is processed in sequence. The function starts with `a` and progressively appends each subsequent element from `xs` until the entire list is consumed.

4. **Termination**: Since the list is processed from the first element to the last, and each recursive call processes a smaller list, the recursion terminates after processing all elements.

5. **Result**: The final result is the initial value `a` with all elements of the list appended in order.

This step-by-step explanation demonstrates that the function `addList` effectively appends all elements of the list to the initial value `a`, treating `a` as the accumulator that receives all elements sequentially.

rag.name: Infinite.exists_superset_card_eq
rag.content:
/-- See `Infinite.exists_subset_card_eq` for a version that provides an arbitrary
`s : Finset α` for any cardinality. -/
theorem exists_superset_card_eq [Infinite α] (s : Finset α) (n : ℕ) (hn : #s ≤ n) :
    ∃ t : Finset α, s ⊆ t ∧ #t = n := by
  induction' n with n IH generalizing s
  · exact ⟨s, subset_refl _, Nat.eq_zero_of_le_zero hn⟩
  · rcases hn.eq_or_lt with hn' | hn'
    · exact ⟨s, subset_refl _, hn'⟩
    obtain ⟨t, hs, ht⟩ := IH _ (Nat.le_of_lt_succ hn')
    obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := exists_not_mem_finset t
    refine ⟨Finset.cons x t hx, hs.trans (Finset.subset_cons _), ?_⟩
    simp [hx, ht]

/-- If every finset in a type has bounded cardinality, that type is finite. -/
noncomputable def fintypeOfFinsetCardLe {ι : Type*} (n : ℕ) (w : ∀ s : Finset ι, #s ≤ n) :
    Fintype ι := by
  apply fintypeOfNotInfinite
  intro i
  obtain ⟨s, c⟩ := Infinite.exists_subset_card_eq ι (n + 1)
  specialize w s
  rw [c] at w
  exact Nat.not_succ_le_self n w

variable {β α : Type*} [Collection β α]
informal_statement: For any element \( z \) and any set \( a \), the set formed by adding \( z \) to \( a \) is finite exactly when \( a \) itself is finite.
informal_proof:
First, we assume that the set \( a \) is finite. When we add an element \( z \) to \( a \), we get a new set \( a' = a \cup \{ z \} \). Since \( a \) is finite and we are only adding one element, \( a' \) remains finite. This shows that if \( a \) is finite, then \( a' \) is also finite.

Next, we consider the converse. Suppose that adding \( z \) to \( a \) results in a finite set \( a' \). Since \( a \subseteq a' \) and \( a' \) is finite, \( a \) must also be finite because a subset of a finite set is finite.

Therefore, the addition of an element preserves the finiteness of the set if and only if the original set was finite.

/-- See `Infinite.exists_subset_card_eq` for a version that provides an arbitrary
`s : Finset α` for any cardinality. -/
theorem exists_superset_card_eq [Infinite α] (s : Finset α) (n : ℕ) (hn : #s ≤ n) :
    ∃ t : Finset α, s ⊆ t ∧ #t = n := by
  induction' n with n IH generalizing s
  · exact ⟨s, subset_refl _, Nat.eq_zero_of_le_zero hn⟩
  · rcases hn.eq_or_lt with hn' | hn'
    · exact ⟨s, subset_refl _, hn'⟩
    obtain ⟨t, hs, ht⟩ := IH _ (Nat.le_of_lt_succ hn')
    obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := exists_not_mem_finset t
    refine ⟨Finset.cons x t hx, hs.trans (Finset.subset_cons _), ?_⟩
    simp [hx, ht]

informal_statement: If set \( b \) is a subset of a finite set \( a \), then \( b \) is finite.
informal_proof: Since \( b \) is a subset of the finite set \( a \), every element in \( b \) is also in \( a \). Because \( a \) has a finite number of elements, \( b \), being a subset, cannot contain more elements than \( a \). Therefore, \( b \) must also be finite.

informal_statement: For any type $α$ and any element $z$ of $α$, and any set $a$ of $α$, the set created by adding $z$ to $a$ using the operation $\texttt{cons}$ is the same as inserting $z$ directly into the set $a$.
informal_proof: Given any type $α$, an element $z$ from $α$, and a set $a$ of elements from $α$, the operation $\texttt{cons}$ (short for "construct") in the context of sets effectively adds the element $z$ to the front of the list that represents the set $a$. However, since sets are unordered collections without duplicates, the act of "consing" $z$ onto $a$ results in a new set that includes $z$ alongside all elements of $a$. This is functionally identical to the operation of inserting $z$ into the set $a$. Therefore, the set formed by $\texttt{cons}\, z\, a$ is equivalent to the set formed by inserting $z$ into $a$.

informal_statement: The set constructed from an empty type is equivalent to the empty set.
informal_proof:
First, we consider the concept of an empty type, which is a type that has no elements. The `set` function in Lean4 constructs a set from a given type. When applied to an empty type `α`, it results in a set that also contains no elements. 

Next, the empty set `∅` is, by definition, the set that contains no elements. Therefore, the set constructed from an empty type and the empty set are both sets that contain no elements. 

By the axiom of extensionality, two sets are considered equal if they contain exactly the same elements. Since both `set (∅ : α)` and `∅` contain no elements, they satisfy the condition of having identical elements. 

Hence, we conclude that the set constructed from an empty type is equal to the empty set.

informal_statement: For any set `a` and element `x`, the set `a` is a subset of the set formed by adding `x` to `a`, denoted as `cons x a`.
informal_proof:
To prove that for any set `a` and element `x`, the set `a` is a subset of `cons x a`, we proceed as follows.

By definition of subset, we need to show that every element `y` in `a` is also in `cons x a`.

According to the lemma `mem_cons_iff`, an element `y` is in `cons x a` if and only if `y` is `x` or `y` is in `a`.

Since we are considering `y` in `a`, we have two cases:

1. **Case 1:** `y` is `x`: In this case, `y` is trivially in `cons x a` because `x` is explicitly included.

2. **Case 2:** `y` is not `x`: Here, since `y` is in `a`, by the lemma `mem_cons_iff`, `y` is also in `cons x a`.

In both cases, `y` is in `cons x a`. Therefore, every element of `a` is in `cons x a`, which means `a` is a subset of `cons x a`.

informal_proof:
First, we consider arbitrary propositions \( a \) and \( b \). 
We can assume that both \( a \) and \( b \) are true, meaning \( a \land b \) is true. 
In such a case, the order in which we list the propositions does not affect their conjunction, so \( b \land a \) is also true. 
Since the conjunction is commutative, the direction holds both ways, thereby proving the equivalence.

informal_statement: The empty set is a subset of any set \( a \). This is because the empty set contains no elements, so any requirement about its elements being in another set \( a \) is trivially satisfied.
informal_proof:
To see why the empty set \( \emptyset \) is a subset of any set \( a \), let's consider the definition of a subset. A set \( b \) is a subset of set \( a \) if every element of \( b \) is also an element of \( a \). Formally, this is written as:
\[
b \subseteq a \iff \forall x (x \in b \implies x \in a)
\]
When \( b \) is the empty set, there are no elements in \( b \). Therefore, there are no elements \( x \) such that \( x \in b \) is true. Since there are no elements to contradict the implication, the statement \( \forall x (x \in \emptyset \implies x \in a) \) is vacuously true. 

Due to this, the condition for \( \emptyset \subseteq a \) is satisfied for any set \( a \). Thus, the empty set is indeed a subset of every set.

<STATEMENT>
For any sets \( A \), \( B \), and \( C \), if \( A \) is a subset of \( B \) and \( B \) is a subset of \( C \), then \( A \) is a subset of \( C \).
</STATEMENT>
<PROOF>
First, we assume that \( A \subseteq B \) and \( B \subseteq C \). By the definition of subset, every element in \( A \) is also in \( B \), and every element in \( B \) is also in \( C \). For any element \( x \) in \( A \), since \( x \) is also in \( B \), and \( x \) is in \( B \), it follows that \( x \) is in \( C \). Therefore, every element of \( A \) is in \( C \), which means \( A \subseteq C \).

/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/

For any propositions \( a \) and \( b \), the conjunction \( a \land b \) is logically equivalent to \( b \land a \). This means that the order in which we state the propositions connected by "and" does not affect the truth value of the compound statement.

<PROOF>

To establish the equivalence of \( a \land b \) and \( b \land a \), we can analyze both directions of the implication independently.

**Forward Direction ( \( a \land b \) implies \( b \land a \) ):**

1. **Assumption**: Assume that \( a \land b \) is true. By the definition of conjunction, both \( a \) and \( b \) must be true individually.
2. **Conclusion**: Since \( b \) and \( a \) are both true, their conjunction \( b \land a \) must also be true. The truth of \( b \land a \) directly follows from the truth of both \( b \) and \( a \).

**Reverse Direction ( \( b \land a \) implies \( a \land b \) ):**

1. **Assumption**: Assume that \( b \land a \) is true. Again, by the definition of conjunction, both \( b \) and \( a \) must be true individually.
2. **Conclusion**: Since \( a \) and \( b \) are both true, their conjunction \( a \land b \) must also be true. The truth of \( a \land b \) directly follows from the truth of both \( a \) and \( b \).

Since both directions have been proven, we conclude that \( a \land b \) is logically equivalent to \( b \land a \). This demonstrates the commutative property of conjunction in propositional logic.

First, we establish that `Finset α` adheres to the subset relation definition, ensuring that for any elements `a` and `b` in `α`, `a ∈ Finset α` and `b ∈ Finset α` if and only if `a ∈ b` within the context of `Finset α`.
  
Next, we confirm that an element `a` does not belong to the empty `Finset`, which is a fundamental property of the membership relation in empty sets.

Finally, we verify that membership in a `Finset` constructed by adding an element to another `Finset` is consistent with the membership relation in the resulting structure, specifically in the case of `a ∈ b-cons c`, ensuring that an element `a` is in `b-cons c` if and only if `a` is in `b` or `a` is equal to `c`.

These properties together confirm that `Finset α` satisfies the criteria to be an instance of the `Collection` structure over `α`.

```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/

informal_statement:
The `Collection` structure for multisets provides the following definitions:
  - A multiset `a` is a subset of another multiset `b` if every element of `a` appears in `b` with at least the same multiplicity (formal definition `subset_iff`).
  - No element is a member of the empty multiset (formal definition `not_mem_empty`).
  - An element `x` is a member of the multiset `y + [x']` (where `y` is another multiset) if and only if `x` is a member of `y` or `x` equals `x'` (formal definition `mem_cons_iff`).
informal_proof:
1. **Subset Relation Definition (`subset_iff`)**:
   - Let `α` be any type.
   - For any two multisets `a` and `b` of type `α`, the subset relation `a ⊆ b` is defined as every element of `a` appearing in `b` with at least the same multiplicity.

2. **Membership in Empty Multiset (`not_mem_empty`)**:
   - By definition, no element can be a member of the empty multiset since it contains no elements.

3. **Membership in Multiset with Head (`mem_cons_iff`)**:
   - For any element `x` and multiset `y` of type `α`, the membership `x ∈ y + [x']` (where `x'` is the head element) is true if and only if `x` is already a member of `y` or `x` is equal to `x'`.

Each of these definitions directly corresponds to the provided Lean4 code, faithfully capturing the informal mathematical understanding of multisets and their operations.
